title: JSON Web Encryption (JWE)
summary: JSON Web Encryption (JWE) represents encrypted content using JSON-based data structures. The cryptographic algorithms and identifiers it uses are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms specification and IANA registries.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON Web Encryption, or JWE, is a way to lock a message so that only the intended reader can open it, and so the reader can tell if anyone changed the message on the way. The locked message is a JSON object, so it travels through programs that already handle JSON.

questions: what is the enc header parameter in jwe
subtitle: Encrypts a message into a JSON object, with a protected header, a wrapped content key and an authentication tag.

tldr.problem: Applications needed a way to encrypt data and prove it was not altered, and to carry that data in JSON without breaking the programs that move it around.
tldr.mechanism: JWE encrypts the plaintext with a fresh content encryption key and adds an authentication tag. The key itself is protected for the recipient, and a JOSE header records the algorithms used and which key to use.
tldr.outcome: Two serializations result: a compact URL-safe string for tight places such as HTTP headers, and a JSON object that can encrypt the same content to several recipients at once. The RFC is a Proposed Standard from May 2015 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7516 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015. It has not been obsoleted and nothing in the unit metadata updates it, so it remains the definition of JSON Web Encryption, alongside RFC 7515 for signatures and RFC 7518 for the algorithms.

sections.title: Encryption as a JSON Object
sections.content:
JSON Web Encryption (JWE) represents encrypted content using JSON-based data structures. Its cryptographic mechanisms encrypt and provide integrity protection for an arbitrary sequence of octets. Integrity protection means the recipient can tell whether the data was altered or damaged on the way.

Two closely related serializations are defined. The JWE Compact Serialization is a compact, URL-safe representation intended for space constrained environments such as HTTP Authorization headers and URI query parameters. The JWE JSON Serialization represents JWEs as JSON objects and enables the same content to be encrypted to multiple parties. Both share the same cryptographic underpinnings.

The algorithms and their identifiers are not defined here. They live in the separate JSON Web Algorithms specification and in the IANA registries it sets up. Related digital signature and message authentication code capabilities are described in the separate JSON Web Signature specification. Names defined by this RFC are short because a core goal is for the resulting representations to be compact.
sections.plainLanguage: JWE locks a message so that only the intended reader can open it and can tell if it was changed. It comes in two shapes: a short string for places where space is tight, and a JSON object that can serve several readers at once.

sections.title: The Pieces of a JWE
sections.content:
A Content Encryption Key (CEK) is the symmetric key used by the content encryption algorithm to turn the plaintext into ciphertext and an authentication tag. The CEK is usually fresh for every message.

JWE uses authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD). An AEAD algorithm encrypts the plaintext, lets extra data be specified, and gives an integrated content integrity check over the ciphertext and that extra data. It takes the plaintext and the Additional Authenticated Data as inputs and produces the ciphertext and the Authentication Tag. The Additional Authenticated Data is an input to the operation that is integrity protected but not encrypted. The Authentication Tag is the output that ensures the integrity of the ciphertext and the Additional Authenticated Data. AES Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is one such algorithm.

The JWE Encrypted Key holds the CEK after it has been protected for the recipient. For some algorithms it is the empty octet sequence. The JWE Initialization Vector is the value used when encrypting the plaintext, and is also the empty octet sequence for algorithms that do not use one.

The way the CEK reaches the recipient is called a Key Management Mode. This specification lists five: Key Encryption, where the CEK is encrypted to the recipient with an asymmetric algorithm; Key Wrapping, where a symmetric key wrapping algorithm protects it; Direct Key Agreement, where a key agreement algorithm agrees the CEK; Key Agreement with Key Wrapping, where key agreement produces a key that wraps the CEK; and Direct Encryption, where the CEK is the symmetric key the two parties already share.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets its own content encryption key. The message is locked with that key, and the key itself is protected separately for the reader. The step that protects the key has five possible shapes, and the header says which one was used.

sections.title: The Values a JWE Holds
sections.content:
A JWE represents six logical values: the JOSE Header, the JWE Encrypted Key, the JWE Initialization Vector, the JWE AAD, the JWE Ciphertext and the JWE Authentication Tag.

The JOSE Header members are the union of the members of three possible values: the JWE Protected Header, the JWE Shared Unprotected Header and the JWE Per-Recipient Unprotected Header. The Protected Header holds the parameters that the authenticated encryption operation integrity protects, and those parameters apply to all recipients. The Shared Unprotected Header holds parameters that apply to all recipients but are not integrity protected. The Per-Recipient Unprotected Header holds parameters for a single recipient, also not integrity protected.

The JWE AAD is an additional value to be integrity protected by the authenticated encryption operation. It can only be present when using the JWE JSON Serialization. The same effect can be achieved in either serialization by including the AAD value as an integrity-protected header parameter, but at the cost of the value being double base64url encoded.

JWE uses authenticated encryption to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of the plaintext and the integrity of the JWE Protected Header and the JWE AAD. In both serializations, the Protected Header, Encrypted Key, Initialization Vector, Ciphertext and Authentication Tag are base64url encoded, since JSON lacks a way to directly represent arbitrary octet sequences.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWE holds six things: a header, the protected key, the starting value for the cipher, the locked text, a tag that proves nothing was changed, and sometimes extra data that is protected but not hidden.

sections.title: The JOSE Header
sections.content:
The header describes the encryption applied to the plaintext and optionally extra properties of the JWE. Header parameter names within the JOSE Header MUST be unique, and the rules about handling parameters that are not understood are the same as in the JSON Web Signature specification.

The alg parameter identifies the cryptographic algorithm used to encrypt, or to determine the value of, the CEK. The encrypted content is not usable if the value does not represent a supported algorithm, or if the recipient has no key that works with it. The enc parameter identifies the content encryption algorithm, which MUST be an AEAD algorithm with a specified key length, and this parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations. The zip parameter names a compression algorithm applied to the plaintext before encryption; the value defined here is DEF, compression with the DEFLATE algorithm. When compression is used, the parameter MUST be integrity protected, so it MUST occur only within the JWE Protected Header.

Five parameters help the recipient find the right key: jku gives the URL of a JWK Set, jwk gives the public key itself, kid gives a key hint, x5u gives the URL of an X.509 certificate or chain, and x5c gives the certificate chain, x5t and x5t#S256 give certificate SHA-1 and SHA-256 thumbprints. Each of them points at the public key to which the JWE was encrypted, so the recipient can work out which private key to use.

Two parameters describe the content: typ names the type of the complete JWE and cty names the type of the secured content. The crit parameter lists the header parameters that a recipient is required to understand.
sections.plainLanguage: The header says which algorithms were used and which key to open the message with. It must name an encryption algorithm that the reader supports, or the message cannot be read.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting
sections.content:
To encrypt, the sender picks the key management mode named in the alg parameter. Where the mode needs a CEK, the sender generates a random one of the length the content encryption algorithm requires, or derives it through key agreement. The CEK is then encrypted or wrapped for the recipient, and that result becomes the JWE Encrypted Key. Where Direct Key Agreement or Direct Encryption are used, the JWE Encrypted Key is the empty octet sequence. A random initialization vector of the right size is generated, or an empty one if the algorithm does not need it.

The sender may compress the plaintext, builds the header objects, and computes the Additional Authenticated Data as the ASCII of the encoded protected header. If a JWE AAD value is present, the Additional Authenticated Data becomes the ASCII of the encoded protected header, a period, and the encoded AAD. The sender then encrypts with the CEK, the initialization vector and that Additional Authenticated Data, producing the ciphertext and the authentication tag.

To decrypt, the receiver reverses the steps. It parses the representation, base64url decodes the parts, checks that the protected header is a valid JSON object, and verifies that it understands every field it is required to support. It then finds the key, decrypts the JWE Encrypted Key to get the CEK, and decrypts the ciphertext while validating the authentication tag. If the tag is incorrect, the receiver rejects the input without emitting any decrypted output. If no recipient succeeded, the JWE MUST be considered invalid.

The RFC also notes that it is an application decision which algorithms may be used in a given context: even if a JWE can be decrypted, unless the algorithms used are acceptable to the application, it SHOULD consider the JWE to be invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender makes a fresh key, protects it for the reader, locks the message and adds a tag. The reader undoes this and checks the tag. If the tag does not match, the reader gets nothing back, not even partial plaintext.

sections.title: Two Serializations
sections.content:
The JWE Compact Serialization represents encrypted content as a compact, URL-safe string: the base64url of the protected header, then a period, then the base64url of the encrypted key, a period, the initialization vector, a period, the ciphertext, and finally a period and the authentication tag. Only one recipient is supported, and the format has no way to hold a shared unprotected header, a per-recipient unprotected header or a JWE AAD value.

The JWE JSON Serialization represents encrypted content as a JSON object, and is neither optimized for compactness nor URL safe. It has two closely related syntaxes. The general syntax can encrypt the content to more than one recipient: the object holds protected, unprotected, iv, aad, ciphertext and tag, plus a recipients array with one element per recipient, each holding that recipient's header and encrypted_key. The flattened syntax drops the recipients array and puts those two members at the top level, which suits the single-recipient case.

All recipients share the same protected header, initialization vector, ciphertext and authentication tag, which can save significant space when the message is large. Therefore all header parameters that specify the treatment of the plaintext must be the same for all recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: One form is a single line of text with dots in it, handy for a header or a web link. The other is a JSON object, which can hold a separate wrapped key for each reader while sharing one locked message.

sections.title: Telling a JWE from a JWS
sections.content:
Several ways tell a JSON Web Encryption object from a JSON Web Signature object, and all of them give the same answer for legal input, though they may differ for malformed input.

In the compact forms, the number of segments differs: a JWS has three segments separated by two periods, and a JWE has five segments separated by four periods. In the JSON forms, the members differ: a JWS has a payload member and a JWE does not, and a JWE has a ciphertext member and a JWS does not.

The header gives two more clues. If the alg value represents a digital signature or message authentication code algorithm, or is the value none, the object is a JWS. If it represents a key encryption, key wrapping, direct key agreement, key agreement with key wrapping or direct encryption algorithm, it is a JWE. And if an enc member exists at all, the object is a JWE.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell an encrypted message from a signed one by counting the dots, by looking for a ciphertext member, or by reading the algorithm name in the header.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the security issues that apply to any cryptographic application must be addressed by JWS, JWE and JWK agents. Among them are protecting the user's asymmetric private and symmetric secret keys, and countering various attacks. All the security considerations in the JSON Web Signature specification apply here, as do those in XML Encryption 1.1 other than the XML specific ones.

Random values are used for content encryption keys and initialization vectors when encrypting, so key entropy matters. Implementations performing encryption must protect the key encryption key and the content encryption key: compromise of the key encryption key may disclose all content protected with that key, and compromise of the content encryption key may disclose the associated content.

Algorithms of matching strengths should be used together whenever possible. When AES Key Wrap is used with a given key size, the same key size is recommended when AES GCM is also used. If the key encryption and content encryption algorithms differ, the effective security is determined by the weaker of the two.

When decrypting, care is needed so the recipient cannot be used as an oracle. An attacker might change the alg value from RSA-OAEP to RSA1_5 to create a formatting error that helps recover the content encryption key, so all formatting errors should be reported as a single error when content is rejected. Restricting a key to a limited set of algorithms also prevents this. To mitigate the attacks described in RFC 3218, the recipient MUST NOT distinguish between format, padding and length errors of encrypted keys, and it is strongly recommended to substitute a randomly generated CEK and carry on when an improperly formatted key arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC warns about three things: keep the keys safe, use algorithms of similar strength, and give the same answer for every kind of broken key so that an attacker cannot learn from the errors. Different errors also take different amounts of time, which leaks information, so the timings should look alike.
